analysis.one_liner: Ends the Interior Secretary's power to waive royalties that oil and gas companies owe on public land.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Energy Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets the Interior Secretary suspend, waive, or reduce the royalties and rents companies pay to drill or mine on public land and offshore waters. This bill would repeal that authority outright, requiring companies to pay the royalties set in their leases no matter what. It was introduced in March 2020 and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the public treasuries that receive federal energy royalties, including states and the Land and Water Conservation Fund, since companies could no longer get their payments reduced or erased.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers owed oil and gas royalties

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the Mineral Leasing Act that lets the Interior Secretary suspend, waive, or reduce rents or royalties on leased public land [S3][S2].
Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Secretary 'may not reduce or eliminate any royalty or net profit share established under a lease' for offshore oil and gas drilling [S3][S2].
Requires companies to pay the royalties written into their leases, keeping public revenue from oil, gas, coal, and other federal minerals flowing to the government [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and other mineral companies that lease public land and offshore tracts, who would lose the ability to have royalty bills lowered or forgiven during price slumps; the same authority also protects leaseholders' ability to pause operations without penalty.

drawbacks.text: The waiver authority was designed as a safety valve: in a price crash or emergency, letting companies pause royalties can keep marginal wells producing rather than shut down, which affects jobs and production in energy-producing communities. Repealing it removes that flexibility entirely [S2].

The bill was narrow: it addressed royalty relief but not the broader terms of federal mineral leases, so companies could still negotiate favorable rates when leases are issued rather than through later waivers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward public money: royalties on federal energy production can run into the billions in normal years, and waivers directly cut that revenue. The cost is real but situational — the authority is most useful during rare price collapses, when a temporary suspension can keep small producers solvent. The bill's design traded that emergency flexibility for a guarantee that lease terms are always honored. Weighing them, the recurring taxpayer benefit outweighs the occasional emergency cost, though a designed-in emergency exception would have blunted the main objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was read and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on March 12, 2020, with Senators Markey and Sanders as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
The CRS summary confirms the bill's single effect: barring the Interior Department from suspending, waiving, or reducing royalties on federal mineral production, including offshore oil and gas [S2].

The bill arrived amid the 2020 oil price collapse, when the Interior Department was using its royalty-relief authority on federal leases, making the timing of the proposal a direct response to that practice.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases benefited, since the authority to suspend or reduce the royalties they owe remained in place and unused authority could be revived at any time.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal royalty waiver authority [S3][S5].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Lisa Murkowski, R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republicans cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Energy Committee never took the bill up [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies on federal lands and offshore leases
industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to get royalties on public resources suspended, waived, or reduced — revenue the government and states would otherwise collect. In the 2020 price collapse, federal leaseholders gained from exactly this relief.

industries.industry: Coal and other Mineral Leasing Act lessees (phosphate, sodium, potassium)
industries.note: The repealed provision covered rents and royalties on all leased public minerals, not just oil and gas, so these leaseholders also would have lost waiver flexibility.
